qs.q: A burn patient develops green-blue pus with a fruity odor. The organism is
qs.e: Pseudomonas produces pyocyanin (blue-green pigment) and pyoverdine giving green-blue pus with a characteristic grape-like or fruity odor. This organism is a common opportunistic pathogen in burn wounds.

qs.q: Green-blue pus with a fruity odor in a burn patient is characteristic of an infection with Pseudomonas aeruginosa. The green color is due to pyocyanin and the fruity odor is due to pyrazinamide production.
qs.e: Pseudomonas aeruginosa is an opportunistic pathogen often associated with hospital-acquired infections, particularly in burn patients. It is known for producing characteristic pigments like pyocyanin (blue-green) and elastase, which contribute to the color and odor of the wound exudate.

ai.subject: Medicine
ai.summary: Burns are tissue injuries from heat, chemicals, electricity or radiation that disrupt skin integrity, fluid balance and immune function. Clinical reasoning focuses on assessing depth, extent, and systemic impact to guide resuscitation, infection control and rehabilitation.

sections.p: A burn is a loss of skin integrity due to an external agent. Diagnosis is clinical, based on appearance, depth, and total body surface area (TBSA).
Severity is staged by depth and TBSA. The Lund‑Browder chart estimates TBSA; the ABCDE system guides resuscitation.
b: First‑degree: superficial epidermis, <10% TBSA; second‑degree: epidermis + dermis, <20% TBSA; third‑degree: full thickness, >20% TBSA

sections.p: Common causes vary by setting. In low‑resource areas, open fire, cooking stoves, kerosene, and electrical accidents are frequent.
b: Thermal: open flame, hot liquids, cooking fires

sections.p: Patients present with pain, erythema, blistering, or dry scarring. Systemic signs include tachycardia, hypotension, and altered mental status.
Investigations confirm extent, rule out complications and guide fluid resuscitation.

t.b: Abnormal values indicate fluid shifts or organ injury

sections.p: Early recognition of shock, inhalation injury, and infection prevents mortality.
Treat the cause, stabilize the patient, prevent infection, and support healing.
b: Secure airway if inhalation injury suspected
Apply sterile dressings, avoid tight bandages
Use broad‑spectrum antibiotics if infection risk high

t.b: Avoid nephrotoxic agents in renal impairment

sections.p: Long‑term care includes wound care, physiotherapy, and psychosocial support. Prevention focuses on safe cooking practices and fire safety.
b: Education on fire safety and safe use of kerosene

sections.p: Differential includes superficial skin infections, allergic dermatitis, and scalds from non‑thermal sources.
Lab values may be falsely normal early in shock; skin blanching may mask underlying depth.
b: Early serum lactate may be low despite hypoperfusion
Dry eschar can hide underlying dermal injury

whenToSeekHelp: Severe hypotension or tachycardia, signs of inhalation injury, extensive TBSA (>20%), altered mental status, signs of infection such as fever or purulent drainage

faq.q: What is the first step in managing a burn patient?
faq.a: Assess airway, breathing, circulation and estimate TBSA for fluid resuscitation.

faq.q: How do you estimate burn size in children?
faq.a: Use the rule of nines or Lund‑Browder chart, adjusting for age and body proportions.

faq.q: When is surgery needed for burns?
faq.a: For full‑thickness burns, graftable areas, or when infection or contracture threatens function.
